title: Don't Minimize the Side Effects
body_text: This is kind of a tough read, but a necessary one. It’s from a Canadian oncologist, on the glossing-over of harms and side effects in oncology trials, and you can sense the frustration from the author. That’s not surprising, because he’s warned about just this issue before, and apparently to little effect. It really is a problem. Everyone knows that cancer treatment is hard on the patients, and frankly there are many drugs in that area with side effects that would be outright unacceptable in most other situations. But patients facing a very high chance of death within (say) 18 months are often willing to put up with a lot, and I can’t sit here and blame them, either. In every case, there are very, very difficult calculations to make: how much longer lifetime are we talking about? With what sorts of side effects and resulting quality of life? As compared to what sort of quality of life with the cancer itself? And what sorts of hardships for everyone around them? No, these are awful situations. But in order to work through those problems, everyone involved needs the real story, and that includes that bad effects from the drugs that have to be factored in. The point of Bishal Gyawali’s articles is that investigator-scored side effects and (especially) their durations are very poorly characterized. There’s also a tendency to lump things together, as in “adverse events of grade 3 or higher” and that sort of thing. It’s especially disturbing to see some things characterized as “well tolerated” when what’s really meant is “well tolerated by the standards of chemotherapy” or “when compared to dying of cancer”. There’s an underlying problem with the framing, too: The present culture considers cancer treatment as a ‘war’ that must be fought and won. This battle metaphor persuades many patients to endure side effects silently, fearing to even mention them to clinicians. Any alteration of treatment to manage side effects is looked upon as giving up on the war, while a response rate of 20% in a trial of 40 patients is celebrated as a breakthrough. War as a metaphor often confuses things more than it clarifies, and that’s been the case for a long time in oncology. . .
